accuracy.evidence: Checked against the National Curriculum in England English programmes of study (Years 5–6: use a thesaurus; select vocabulary for meaning; formal and informal vocabulary, Appendix 2), Common Core L.4.5c, L.5.5c and L.5.4c, and the Merriam-Webster and Oxford Learner's thesaurus entries for bright (shining vs intelligent senses), thin (slim, slender, skinny, bony, scrawny), cool (cold vs calm senses) and angry (annoyed, cross, furious). Connotation and intensity labels follow the learner dictionaries' usage notes (skinny and scrawny often disapproving; slender approving; scorching = very hot). Jubilant, poky and compact meanings checked in Merriam-Webster.

misconceptions.evidence: Targets the documented thesaurus slips teachers report: choosing from the wrong sense (step 1 prediction 'dazzling pupil', m2 cool/calm, challenge Q1 and Q6 'calm' for a cool drink), treating synonyms as identical (step 3 prediction on warm/hot/scorching, m3), ignoring connotation (step 2 prediction skinny vs slender for gran, p2, m6 poky), wrong register (step 4 sort, p4, m4, challenge Q3 'grab'/'get loads of'), wrong intensity (challenge Q4 furious/livid for a little cross), and over-swapping every repeated word (m5 exclaimed), plus using an unknown word unchecked (m7).

lab_distinct.evidence: flagthes models a thesaurus entry: sentences are dragged onto numbered sense groups of one headword, synonyms are placed on a kind–plain–unkind connotation scale, shuffled synonyms are tapped into a weakest-to-strongest ladder, words are sorted by register (letter to the head vs chat), and speech verbs are dragged into sentences whose clues decide the fit. No other lab works with sense groups, connotation and intensity of synonyms; flagshade (Shades of Meaning) only orders verbs of one meaning by strength and flagidiom sorts literal and figurative phrases; neither uses sense groups, connotation or register, and lab_distinct stayed under 30%.

lab_teaches.evidence: The learner discovers each check from feedback: filing 'Priya is a bright pupil' under shining returns 'A pupil who learns fast is clever, not glowing. Dazzling would sound silly here'; putting slim under unkind says 'Slim and slender sound kind'; tapping scorching first says 'warm comes first: it is the weakest one left'; putting kids under the letter says it is too chatty for the head teacher; choosing asked for the car warning says 'asked goes with a question, but the clue is a warning and an exclamation mark'.

predictions.evidence: Three predictions with a tempting wrong option: dazzling can replace bright in 'bright pupil' because it is listed (sorting shows it is the shining sense), skinny for describing gran kindly (the scale places skinny under unkind), and warm/hot/scorching mean exactly the same because they are synonyms (the ladder makes the learner order them by strength).

challenge_feedback.evidence: Six questions with tagged wrong options and a message naming the slip: wrong sense ('dazzling belongs to a different sense of the headword'), unkind feeling (skinny, scrawny), too chatty for a formal letter (grab, get loads of), too strong (furious, livid, freezing), and verbs that do not match the clues (whispered, muttered for someone stuck shouting Help!).

readability.evidence: validate_lessons passes the kid (≤ 6.5) and adult (≤ 9.5) limits. Kid paragraphs give one check each (sense, feeling and strength, reader) with a concrete pair (bright sun / bright pupil, slim / skinny, purchase / grab). The lab uses the same terms as the curriculum: synonym, headword, sense, formal, chatty.

no_filler.evidence: No filler pattern matches. Each lab step teaches one check, the step text says what to do in one or two sentences, and every item explanation states why the right word fits and why each distractor does not, for example 'Chilled and chilly are about temperature'.

mobile.evidence: Screenshots at 360 px (touch, 1.5x) in light and dark for every step before and after Show me: sentence cards wrap inside the card, the two sense boxes and three scale boxes fit in one row, placed words wrap inside their box (fixed after the first screenshots showed 'skinny, bony, scrawny' running past the unkind box), and the feedback box wraps above the button row.

accessibility.evidence: Every canvas action has a button: Sense 1 and Sense 2, kind/plain/unkind with labels such as 'slim is kind', each ladder word ('Next weakest: hot'), letter/chat, and each speech verb. The canvas aria-label reads the current sentence or word and the feedback after every move, challenge feedback is an aria-live status, and axe (WCAG 2.1 AA) is clean in both themes on desktop and iPhone 13.
